concept: Search node tier sizing for vector indexes
summary: Source-anchored research for Search node tier sizing for vector indexes. Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: HighLevel's May 4, 2026 engineering account reports that scalar and binary quantization improved MongoDB retrieval latency and memory pressure, but quantization did not resolve its broader workload architecture problems; scalar preserved quality better in its tests. The account does not establish a reproducible Search Node tier capacity because it omits the necessary dedicated-node hardware and index configuration. (low confidence)

Use Search System Memory, Search Index Size, Search Page Faults, and Search Normalized Process CPU together to diagnose capacity. MongoDB recommends page faults near zero for the intended resident search working set and waiting for indexing, segment merging, and flushing to settle before performance tests. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)

Automatic quantization reduces resident vector-index memory by approximately 3.75x for scalar and 24x for binary, including graph overhead; the 4x and 32x raw-vector ratios are not whole-index sizing ratios. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30)

MongoDB recommends approximately 4:1 storage-to-RAM capacity for scalar quantization and 24:1 for binary; it also recommends free disk space equal to 125% of estimated quantized index size. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30)

For its 15.3M-vector, 2048-dimensional binary benchmark, MongoDB lists 5.1 GB RAM and 155.04 GB storage requirements and uses S30-high-cpu nodes with 8 GB RAM, 213 GB disk and four vCPUs each. This is a measured configuration, not a guarantee for every equally sized corpus. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30)

TitanBases reports scalar quantization reduced index memory from 4.51 GiB to 1.36 GiB but reduced Recall@10 from 99.37% to 92.83% and Exact Match@10 from 94.88% to 41.22% in its controlled accuracy test. Its separate 10M-vector performance environment does not establish that these memory figures apply to 10M vectors. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-02)

For automatic quantization, size the in-memory working set separately from the complete on-disk index. MongoDB documents approximate effective RAM reductions of 3.75x for scalar and 24x for binary quantization; these are smaller than raw-value compression factors because graph overhead remains. Full-precision vectors remain on disk for rescoring or exact search. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)

MongoDB's deployment guidance suggests approximate storage-to-RAM ratios of 4:1 for scalar and 24:1 for binary quantization, estimates binary-index disk size with rescoring as original index size multiplied by 25/24, and recommends free disk space equal to 125% of estimated index size. These are capacity estimates, not latency guarantees. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)

Independent CWI research found that the best-performing CPU depends on vector index, quantization, and memory-access patterns even with the same 64 GB RAM and eight vCPUs. Its experiments used FAISS and USearch with individual queries, not Atlas; use it to justify benchmarking CPU choices, not to assign performance equivalence to Atlas tier names. (low confidence)

HighLevel reports that quantization improved memory and tail latency but served only as a stopgap for its large shared-corpus retrieval workload. This production account scopes the idea that shrinking an index alone solves tenant skew, filtering and capacity problems; it does not establish a general Atlas tier limit. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-05-04)

An independent 75M-vector experiment isolated a single binary index, stopped competing work and warmed the working set before measuring latency. It explicitly limits the result to that warm configuration, illustrating why a warm-query benchmark cannot alone size cold-start and concurrent-indexing capacity. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-08-01)

Match the node class to the binding resource: MongoDB positions Low-CPU nodes as a starting point for nonquantized vector workloads, High-CPU nodes for high query throughput or quantized workloads requiring more compute, and storage-optimized nodes for large quantized indexes with moderate compute demand. Lower memory requirements can expose a disk-capacity limit. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)

Percona's October 29, 2026 benchmark used self-managed Percona Search for MongoDB, not Atlas Search Node tiers, on one host and one corpus. Its memory and concurrency measurements are useful methodological evidence, but cannot be substituted for Atlas tier sizing or a managed-service SLA. (low confidence)

Size the Search tier from the vector-index working set, storage and CPU demand rather than the database document count alone; dedicated Search Nodes let search resources scale separately from the database tier. (medium confidence)

MongoDB's production-sizing guidance recommends node RAM at least 10% above total vector-index size and explains that nearly 90% of dedicated Search Node RAM can serve vector data and indexes. For quantized indexes, interpret this alongside the separate required-memory estimate rather than treating the complete disk footprint as resident RAM. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)

Automatic quantization retains full-precision vectors on disk for exact search and binary rescoring. Budget both representations and the graph; memory reduction does not imply equivalent disk savings. (medium confidence)

In the AWS benchmark configuration, low-CPU nodes have roughly 6:1 disk-to-memory capacity; high-CPU and storage-optimized nodes have roughly 25:1. High-CPU suits demanding QPS or quantization, whereas storage-optimized offers high storage capacity with fewer CPUs. These profiles are workload starting points. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30)

Binary quantization can reduce the memory tier while rescoring and higher candidate counts consume throughput capacity. MongoDB observed higher scalar QPS in its concurrent benchmark; choose node CPU capacity using representative recall, concurrency and latency targets. (medium confidence)

Increasing Search Node count provides more query-serving resources; it does not automatically divide a replica-set index into smaller independent pieces. MongoDB provisions Search Nodes per shard, so adding replicas and partitioning the corpus are different sizing decisions. (low confidence)

Size dedicated Search Nodes independently of the database cluster: a search tier supplies RAM, local storage, and CPU, while the number of Search Nodes controls additional query-serving capacity. MongoDB's vector benchmark kept an M20 base cluster while changing Search Node configurations. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)

Fitting the index in RAM does not establish sufficient query capacity. MongoDB documents additional CPU demand from vector indexing and exact search, and warns that simultaneous indexing and querying can contend for resources. Size and test the CPU budget under representative ingestion and query traffic. (medium confidence)

A node comparison must hold retrieval quality and workload shape explicit: MongoDB's benchmark measures recall against full-precision exact results and tests concurrency; Percona's controlled benchmark reports throughput at recall floors and demonstrates that client-harness behavior can invalidate concurrency interpretations. This supports measuring recall, tail latency, and achieved server concurrency before attributing a throughput ceiling to node size. (medium confidence)

MongoDB's benchmark overview explicitly states that horizontal Search Node scaling, although recommended for higher throughput, was not measured in those tests. Its published results therefore do not establish a linear throughput multiplier for adding nodes. (low confidence)
